To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the promotion of brain games is characterized by the deployment of three key strategies: the deployment of expertise, the deployment of risk, and the deployment of third parties.

brain games are promoted as an effective and affordable means to improve cognition and to prevent dementia, and that they do so by deploying expertise, risk metrics and corroboration to intervene in cognitive health.

the promotion of brain games is a complex, multi-layered process, involving multiple actors, including the game developers, the game players, and the game players’ friends and family, as well as other stakeholders, such as health professionals, the media, and government agencies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the politics of brain games, which is to say the ways in which these technologies are implicated in the management and control of ageing and cognitive health.
how the brain games industry is making the brain a ‘site of intervention’ in ways that both enable and constrain ageing and identity work in late life.
the ways in which brain training technologies, as ‘interventions’, are implicated in the production of older adults as ‘subjects’ of health and well-being.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
brain training technologies have the potential to both enhance and constrain older people’s lives.
brain games are not only a product of neoliberalism, but also that they contribute to its ongoing reproduction.
brain training technologies have the capacity to both empower and constrain the ageing process, but that the latter may ultimately be more dominant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
brain training is a form of biopolitics that is not just a matter of life and death, but of life and identity.
the politics of brain games are not so much about ‘use it or lose it’ but rather ‘use it or be lost’.
we are witnessing an emergent ‘brainware’ culture that, in its current form, is not only failing to challenge but also reproducing the very inequalities it claims to redress.
The main takeaway from our work is that

brain games are a form of ‘neuromarketing’ that are both a symptom and an agent of the neoliberalization of later life, which is a process whereby the ‘self’ is increasingly expected to take personal responsibility for their own health and well-being.
the brain games industry is a powerful and influential actor in shaping how ageing and the brain are understood in contemporary Western societies.
brain training is not simply a ‘product’ that can be bought and consumed, but rather, a set of technologies and practices that are deeply embedded in the politics of ageing.
